description: Bhimakali Temple stands in Sarahan, in Rampur tehsil of Shimla district, Himachal Pradesh, about 180 km from Shimla. It is dedicated to Bhimakali, a form of the goddess Durga, who was the presiding deity and kuldevi of the rulers of the former Bushahr state. The temple is built in the tower-temple and kath-kuni style and is described as blending Hindu and Buddhist construction traditions. The complex has three courtyards, with a Narsingha temple in the first, a Raghunath temple in the second and the twin-tower sanctum of Bhimakali in the third. Traditional accounts date the shrine to the 13th century, and Raja Padam Singh contributed to a rebuilding in the 1920s. Local tradition links the site to the fall of Sati's ear and counts it among the 51 Shakta pithas. Press reports in 2023 and 2024 mention a sinking portion of the temple foundation and a structural assessment by IIT Mandi; check with the temple trust for the current position.

description: Bijli Mahadev is a Shiva temple at Kashawri village above the Kullu valley in Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, at an altitude of about 2,460 m, built in the traditional Pahari kath-kuni style. Its name means Lord of Lightning. According to local belief, lightning strikes the Shivalinga from time to time, splitting it, after which the priest reassembles the pieces using butter and a paste of ground pulses and cereals. A tall deodar-wood pole, reported to be about 60 ft high, stands before the temple, and the Beas river can be seen from the premises. Local tradition offers several origin stories, including Shiva's victory over a demon who threatened to flood the valley, and a belief that the Pandavas built the shrine. Devotees come especially in the month of Shravan, and special pujas are held on Maha Shivratri. The shrine is reached by road and a short trek of about 3 km from the last motorable point.

description: Shri Chamunda Nandikeshwar Dham, commonly called Chamunda Devi Temple, is at Padar (Dadh) in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, on the bank of the Baner river, about 15 km from Dharamshala. It is dedicated to Chamunda, a form of Durga, and also honours Shiva as Nandikeshwar. The name recalls the Devi Mahatmya account in which the goddess slays the demon generals Chanda and Munda. The present temple is estimated by the Kangra district administration to be between 400 and 700 years old. Local legend holds that a king and a priest asked the goddess to move from the remote hilltop shrine of Aadi Himani Chamunda, and that she directed them in a dream to the present site, where her image was found. The temple is run by the Shri Chamunda Ji Mandir Trust under state temple administration. Festivals include Chaitra and Sharad Navratri, and the trust provides free community meals.

description: Chintpurni is a town in Una district, Himachal Pradesh, about 40 km north of Una. Its shrine is dedicated to Mata Chintpurni, identified with Chhinnamasta, the headless form of the goddess, and the sanctum holds a round stone pindi. It is counted among the Shakta pithas associated with the story of Sati; accounts differ on what is said to have fallen here. Tradition credits Pandit Mai Das, a Saraswat Brahmin from Patiala state, with establishing the shrine at Chhaproh village about twelve generations ago, and his descendants serve as the temple priests. Four Shiva temples are said to guard the four directions around the goddess. Large fairs are held during the Navratras in Shravan, Ashwin and Chaitra. The temple is managed by the Maa Chintpurni Temple Trust, which operates under Himachal Pradesh government control; press reports say the district Deputy Commissioner heads such trusts.

description: Gurdwara Manikaran Sahib, formally Gurdwara Shri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, is at Manikaran on the right bank of the Parvati river in Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, at an altitude of roughly 1,740 to 1,760 m and roughly 45 km from Kullu. Sikh tradition, drawing on Janamsakhi accounts, says Guru Nanak Dev Ji came here with Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala during his third udasi, and that hot water appeared when he lifted a rock so food could be cooked. According to SikhiWiki, Saint Narayan Hari settled at Manikaran in 1940 and died in 1991, and the gurdwara is run by his daughter and son-in-law. description: Gurdwara Paonta Sahib stands on the bank of the Yamuna river at Paonta Sahib, a town in Sirmaur district, Himachal Pradesh, near the boundary with Uttarakhand. It commemorates Guru Gobind Singh Ji, who came here at the invitation of Raja Medini Prakash of Sirmaur and stayed for about four years, a period Wikipedia gives as four and a half. SikhiWiki records that he kept a court of poets who translated classical texts, and that the first battle he fought, at Bhangani, took place in this period. Sikh tradition explains the name Paonta, meaning foot, either as the place where he first stepped or from a lost ankle ornament. Gobind Ghat leads to the river and a separate Gurdwara Sri Kavi Darbar marks the poetry gatherings. According to SikhiWiki, an eleven-member committee with the SGPC president as ex-officio chairman administers the shrine (check current arrangements with the gurdwara), and a museum holds items linked to the Guru.

description: Jakhoo Temple crowns Jakhu Hill, the highest point of Shimla in Himachal Pradesh, at roughly 2,450 m (about 8,050 ft); published sources give slightly different figures. It is dedicated to Hanuman and lies about 2.5 km east of the Ridge. According to local tradition, Hanuman met the sage Yaku while going to fetch the sanjeevani herb during the Ramayana, and Yaku later raised the shrine in his honour. Troops of monkeys around the temple are regarded by devotees as his descendants. A 33 m (108 ft) Hanuman statue below the temple, begun in 2008 and inaugurated in 2010, was gifted to the state by the HC Nanda Charitable Trust and is visible across much of the town. Visitors reach the hill on foot, by horse or taxi, or by the Jakhu Ropeway, which opened in 2017.

description: Jwalamukhi, a town in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, is a shrine to the goddess Jwala, regarded as a form of Durga or Shakti. Instead of an image, devotees worship natural flames that rise from fissures in the rock of the sanctum; Wikipedia describes the gas as combustible natural gas, while the district administration says worshippers see about nine flames as forms of the Goddess. Tradition links the site to Sati's tongue and counts it among the Shakti Peethas. The earliest surviving text naming the place is the 14th-century Tarikh-i-Firuz-Shahi. According to local tradition, Emperor Akbar failed to extinguish the flames, and Maharaja Ranjit Singh later contributed to the temple. Wikipedia describes the main shrine building as having a golden dome. The district site places it roughly 30 km from Kangra and 56 km from Dharamshala. The temple is administered under the Himachal Pradesh government's temple administration, in which the Kangra Deputy Commissioner serves as Commissioner (Temple).

description: Kangra Fort stands on a hillock between the Manjhi and Banganga rivers near Kangra town in Himachal Pradesh, beneath the Dhauladhar range. It is traditionally associated with the Katoch dynasty of Rajputs. Wikipedia places the earliest surviving structures, a Jain and a Hindu temple, in about the 9th-10th century CE. Its first firm historical mention is Mahmud of Ghazni's raid in 1009; the Tughlaqs, Mughals, Sikhs under Maharaja Ranjit Singh and the British held it in turn, and the 4 April 1905 earthquake left much of it in ruins. Inside, a Svetambara Jain shrine houses an Rishabhanatha image whose pedestal inscription is read as 854 CE, and stone shrines to Ambika Devi and Lakshmi-Narayana are recorded in a courtyard entered through the Darsani Darwaza. The Archaeological Survey of India protects the fort, The Katoch royal family runs the Maharaja Sansar Chand Museum, according to The Tribune.

description: Kinnaur Kailash, also called Kinner Kailash, is a mountain in Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh, given by Wikipedia as about 6,050 m, with the neighbouring Jorkanden peak higher at roughly 6,473 m. Hindus regard it as a winter abode of Shiva, and Buddhist Kinnauris also revere it. A tall natural rock pillar on the massif, known as the Shivling, is described by Wikipedia as standing at about 4,800 m; some trek operators describe it as worshipped as self-manifested (swayambhu). Wikipedia counts the peak among the Panch Kailash, the five Kailash mountains of Hindu tradition, and it is sometimes confused with Mount Kailash in Tibet. Pilgrims travel on foot on the Kinner Kailash yatra. In recent years it has been organised in summer by the Kinnaur district administration, with registration and a medical fitness certificate; dates are announced each year and can be postponed for safety. The 2026 yatra was postponed once on 28 June 2026 for route hazards and later held, with extensions, in July and August. Check Kinnaur district administration notices before planning a visit.

description: Masrur is a rock-cut temple complex in the Kangra valley, Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, carved from a single sandstone ridge facing the Dhauladhar range. According to art historian Michael Meister, cited on Wikipedia, it dates from the first half of the 8th century; a Tribune article places it in the 7th-8th century, and other scholars have proposed later dates. Built in the north Indian latina style, it has a central spire ringed by smaller ones in a plan Meister relates to the Kailasa, the mountain abode of Shiva, and it is often compared with the rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora; a rectangular pool lies in front. The sculpture is mainly Shaiva but also includes Vishnu, Devi and Surya, along with composite forms such as Harihara and Ardhanarishvara. Counts of the original spires vary between 13 and 15 in early surveys, and the work appears unfinished. Accounts of the damage from the 1905 Kangra earthquake differ: some report that the front mandapa and portico fell, others that the monolith was largely spared. Local tradition credits the Pandavas, an attribution scholars do not accept. It is a monument protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

description: Mata Kuan Rani Temple, whose name is usually rendered as the Princess of the Well Temple, stands beside the Beas River in Mandi town, Himachal Pradesh. According to Wikipedia, it is held sacred by both Tibetan Buddhists and Hindus and is linked to Princess Mandarava of Zahor, who became a disciple and consort of Padmasambhava, also known as Guru Rinpoche. In that account her father, King Arshadhara, sentenced the pair to death by fire; the fire is said to have burned for seven days before a lake with a lotus appeared, a miracle linked with Rewalsar, about 24 km from Mandi. The temple is a slate-roofed structure built over a deep well. Another popular telling, recorded by a Hindu heritage blog, names the princess as Tara and describes the couple being buried alive, after which she is revered as the goddess Tara Devi. Tibetan pilgrims and traders are said to have visited often before the borders closed after the Chinese takeover of Tibet.

description: Naina Devi Temple crowns a hilltop in Bilaspur district, Himachal Pradesh, close to the Punjab border and about 20 to 30 km from Anandpur Sahib, depending on the source. According to local tradition it is one of the Shakti Peethas, the sites where parts of Sati's body are said to have fallen; here her eyes are believed to have fallen, which is held to explain the name. Another account, recorded on Wikipedia, tells of a Gurjar boy who found a stone on which a white cow let down milk, after which Raja Bir Chand of Bilaspur built a shrine; Himachal Tourism dates that construction to the 8th century. The hill looks over the Bhakra Dam, Anandpur Sahib and Gobind Sagar lake. Pilgrims reach the shrine by road and then steps; a cable car from the base is also reported, so check current operation locally. Large fairs are held during the Navratri periods and on Shravan Ashtami. According to the Himachal Pradesh government's list of notified temples, the state took over the temple's management in December 1985, and a temple trust now runs it.

description: Shikari Devi Temple sits on Shikari Peak in the Shikari Devi Sanctuary above Janjehli and Karsog, in Mandi district, Himachal Pradesh. description: Akal Takht Sahib stands inside the Darbar Sahib complex in Amritsar, directly facing Harmandir Sahib. It was reconstructed afterwards, and Wikipedia dates the present building to 1995. Sikhs regard it as the supreme temporal seat of the Khalsa, where the Jathedar issues edicts and where Sarbat Khalsa gatherings have historically been convened.

description: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur marks the place on the Ravi where, in Sikh tradition, Guru Nanak settled in about 1504, farmed, and taught for roughly eighteen years until his passing in 1539. Wikipedia records that the present gurdwara was begun in 1925 with funds from Maharaja Bhupinder Singh of Patiala, repaired by the Government of Pakistan in 1995 and fully restored in 2004. Dawn reports that after Guru Nanak's death, Sikhs and Muslims each honoured him by their own rites, and both a samadhi and a grave remain on the site. Indian pilgrims could for years only view it from the Indian side near Dera Baba Nanak; the Kartarpur Corridor opened on 9 November 2019, allowing Indian pilgrims visa-free access, and the grounds were expanded to 42 acres. The corridor has been suspended on the Indian side since May 2025 on security grounds, and as of late October 2026 reports say it remains closed, so visits are not currently possible by this route.

description: Belur Math stands on the west bank of the Hooghly River in Belur, Howrah district, and serves as the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Math and Ramakrishna Mission. description: The Dakshineswar Kali Temple lies on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River at Dakshineswar, in the northern part of Greater Kolkata. description: Kalighat Kali Temple stands in the Kalighat neighbourhood of south Kolkata and is dedicated to the goddess Kali, one of the ten Mahavidyas. Shakta tradition counts it among the 51 Shakti Peethas, holding that the toes of Sati's right foot fell here after her body was dismembered. The shrine is referred to in medieval Bengali texts such as the Mansar Bhasan, though the building seen today is far newer: according to Wikipedia, construction began in 1798 and was finished in 1809 under the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family, whose traditional patronage of the deity is disputed. Kali Puja, Durga Puja, Poila Baisakh and the new-moon days are among the busiest occasions. A major renovation was completed in 2024.

description: Navadwip (Nabadwip) is a town in Nadia district, West Bengal, on the Bhagirathi-Hooghly near its meeting with the Jalangi. description: Alarnath Temple stands at Brahmagiri, roughly 23 km from Puri in Odisha, and is dedicated to Vishnu, with a shrine to his consort Mahalakshmi. It is best known for its link to the Anasara period that follows Snana Yatra, when the Jagannath images in Puri are withdrawn from public view. Devotees who cannot see Jagannath then come here, where, in local belief, the Lord appears as Alarnath. Wikipedia connects the site with the Vaishnava teacher Ramanujacharya's visit to Odisha and with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who is said to have been directed here during Anavasara; a stone where he held sankirtana is preserved. The temple is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of the Sri Vaishnava tradition. Daily offerings include morning bhoga and midday and night food offerings, and the kheeri bhoga given to Alarnath is especially sought by pilgrims. The Orissa High Court issued darshan-management directions for the temple in June 2023, reflecting the crowds of the Anasara season.

description: Biraja Temple in Jajpur, Odisha, is dedicated to Devi Durga worshipped as Biraja (also spelled Viraja), and the Jajpur area is traditionally known as Viraja Kshetra. description: The Jagannath Temple in Puri, on Odisha's coast, is dedicated to Jagannath, a form of Vishnu, worshipped with his siblings Balabhadra and Subhadra as wooden images that are renewed in the Nabakalevara ritual every 8, 12 or 19 years. Tradition credits King Indradyumna with the first temple, while Wikipedia says the present complex was largely rebuilt from the 11th to 12th century under Anantavarman Chodaganga of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. The Kalinga-style main tower rises about 65 metres and carries the Nila Chakra. Puri is counted among the four Char Dham pilgrimage sites with Badrinath, Dwarka and Rameswaram. The Ratha Yatra, in which the deities are drawn on chariots to the Gundicha Temple, is the best-known festival, alongside Snana Yatra and Anavasara. description: The Konark Sun Temple, in Konark on the Bay of Bengal coast in Puri district, Odisha, is dedicated to Surya, the sun god. Wikipedia attributes it to King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty and dates it to about 1250 CE, noting that an earlier sun shrine may have stood here. Built in the Kalinga style, the temple is conceived as a colossal stone chariot with 24 carved wheels, some of which can be used as sundials, drawn by seven horses. The main tower has long since collapsed, but the assembly hall (jagamohana) and the dance hall (nata mandira) survive. UNESCO inscribed the monument as a World Heritage Site in 1984. The Archaeological Survey of India maintains the site and a museum holding fallen sculptures. Incredible India also describes a gate flanked by lions crushing elephants.

description: Lingaraj Temple stands in the old town of Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and is dedicated to Shiva as Lingaraja, the lord of the lingam. Bhubaneswar's older name, Ekamra Kshetra, is explained through the Ekamra Purana, which places the deity beneath a mango tree. Historians generally assign the present structure to the 11th century, crediting the Somavamshi dynasty, with the Ganga rulers later adding to it and introducing Vaishnava elements, so the sanctum is also associated with Hari-Hara. It is a Kalinga-style deula with four aligned parts: the sanctum tower, an assembly hall, a festival hall and an offering hall. The tower is commonly given as about 55 metres (180 ft), and the walled compound holds dozens of smaller shrines. Shivaratri is the major annual festival. Only Hindus may enter; visitors of other faiths can view the exterior from a platform outside the compound wall. The Archaeological Survey of India and a temple trust board are named as its custodians.

description: Mukteshvara Temple is a small Shiva temple in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, usually dated to the 10th century and associated with the Somavamshi period. The Archaeological Survey of India's documentation describes a curvilinear rekha-type sanctum tower paired with a pidha jagamohana whose roof rises in stepped tiers, built of ochre sandstone and set on a low platform. Its exterior is richly carved with female figures, scrollwork, chaitya-window motifs and everyday scenes, and the interior ceiling of the hall bears an eight-petalled lotus medallion with images of the Matrikas. The ornamental arched gateway, the torana, is often singled out as a notable feature; it is dated by some accounts to about 900 CE and is said to show Buddhist architectural influence. An octagonal wall encloses the compound. Scholars disagree on the exact date: figures from about 875 to 975 CE appear, and the attribution to King Yayati I is not universally accepted.

description: Gundicha Temple is a Kalinga-style temple standing in a walled garden in Puri, Odisha, about 3 km from the Jagannath Temple at the far end of the Bada Danda, the grand avenue used for the Rath Yatra. It is best known as the destination of that annual festival, when the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra are drawn on their chariots from the main temple and stay here before returning, a sojourn of about seven full days, or nine days counting the days of arrival and return. Outside the festival the temple is described as largely unused. The complex has a sanctum, assembly hall, festival hall and offering hall, plus a connected kitchen, and is built of light-grey sandstone. Its name is traditionally linked to Queen Gundicha, wife of the legendary King Indradyumna. The deities enter by the western gate and leave by the eastern Nakachana gate.

description: Sakhigopal Temple, formally the Satyabadi Gopinatha Temple, lies in the town of Sakhigopal on the Bhubaneswar-Puri highway in Odisha. The presiding deity is Gopinatha, a form of Krishna, who is also called Sakshi Gopala, the witness Gopala. Local tradition tells of a poor young man and a village headman's daughter: after the headman, who had travelled on pilgrimage with the young man, went back on a promise of marriage, the young man asked Gopala to appear as witness. According to the legend, the deity agreed on condition that the young man not look back, and became a stone image when he did. The temple is described as medieval and built in the Kalinga style. The main festival is Anla Navami, when devotees are permitted to touch the feet of the Radha image, an occasion that draws very large crowds.

description: Tara Tarini Temple is a Shakta shrine on the Kumari hills beside the Rushikulya river near Purushottampur in Ganjam district, Odisha, roughly 28 km from Brahmapur (Berhampur). It honours the twin goddesses Tara and Tarini, who are worshipped as the Sthana (breast) Peetha of Sati, and it is traditionally counted among four major Shakti peethas of Odisha tradition. Its origins are credited to the Kalinga rulers in ancient times, with a 17th-century phase of work attributed to Basupraharaj; a news report also describes the present temple as 17th century. Pilgrims climb about 999 steps to the hilltop shrine, and the temple is administered by the Tara Tarini Development Board. The Chaitra Yatra, held on Tuesdays of the Hindu month of Chaitra, is a major annual gathering. In 2025 the Odisha government announced a Rs 68 crore programme to improve facilities such as the steps, guest accommodation and riverbed.

description: The Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya in Gaya district, Bihar, marks the place where, in Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama attained supreme enlightenment and became the Buddha. UNESCO records that Emperor Ashoka raised the first shrine here and that the brick temple standing today dates to the 5th-6th centuries, the late Gupta period, making it one of the earliest large brick temples in the subcontinent; its carved stone balustrades are an early example of relief sculpture. The complex was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2002. It remains a living place of pilgrimage. According to the Bodhgaya Temple Management Committee, Buddhists held the site until the early 13th century; from 1590 a Shaiva mahant settled there and claimed to be its heir. In 1949 the Government of Bihar passed the Bodhgaya Temple Act, which created the Bodhgaya Temple Management Committee, and the mahant handed over management to it in 1953. UNESCO records that the committee manages the property under that Act. The arrangement of the committee has been debated by some Buddhist groups; the current position should be checked before adding detail.

description: The Mundeshwari Devi Temple stands on Mundeshwari Hill of the Kaimur plateau at Ramgarh village in Kaimur district, Bihar, near the Son river. Built of stone on a rare octagonal plan, it is considered an early example of Nagara-style architecture in Bihar; its original tower is lost and a roof was added later. The presiding deity is Mundeshwari, a form of Durga shown ten-armed on a buffalo, and the sanctum also holds a four-faced Shiva linga. Images of Ganesha, Surya and Vishnu are also found at the temple. The temple's age is disputed. The Bihar State Religious Trust Board and a 2008 seminar in Patna have put it at 108 CE, based on an inscription read as dated in the Shaka era, while the ASI plaque is reported to say 635 CE. Historians generally place the surviving elements in the 6th-7th centuries and suggest the present shrine may be later, built partly from older material. The Archaeological Survey of India has protected the site since 1915. Worship is said to be continuous, and Ramnavami, Shivratri and a Navaratri fair draw pilgrims.

description:
Jal Mandir, the Water Temple, is a Jain shrine at Pawapuri (also called Apapapuri, 'the sinless town') in Nalanda district, Bihar. Jain tradition holds that Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, attained nirvana here at the age of 72 on the night of Diwali, in Kartik, while spending the monsoon retreat in the town, and that he was cremated at this spot. According to a popular account, devotees carried away so much sacred soil from the cremation site that a large hollow formed and filled with water; the temple was later built inside the resulting pond. Tradition credits Mahavira's elder brother, King Nandivardhana, with building the original temple.
The white marble shrine rises from the water in the form of a vimana and houses Mahavira's footprints (charan paduka) for worship. A stone bridge about 180 metres long links it to the bank. The surrounding tank, known for its lotuses, covers about 84 bighas. Pilgrims gather at Diwali to mark the nirvana.

description: Rajgir, in Nalanda district, Bihar, is among the significant pilgrimage centres of Jainism, set among five hills mentioned in the Jain canonical text Aupapatika Sutra. Jain tradition holds that Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, spent about 14 years in the Rajgir-Nalanda region and passed many rainy-season retreats here (sources give differing counts), and that his eleven chief disciples (ganadharas) attained liberation on these hills. King Shrenika, also known as Bimbisara, is remembered as a devoted follower. Rajgir is also regarded as the birthplace of Munisuvrata, the 20th Tirthankara, and four of his five auspicious life events are associated with it; a temple dedicated to him, said to be about 1,200 years old, is still in worship. Jain temples were built on several of the hills, and other sites include a temple at the foot of the hills, the Naulakha temple, and the Son Bhandar caves, which are associated with Jainism and dated to roughly the 3rd-4th century CE. Rajgir is equally associated with the Buddha, so the town is significant to both traditions.

description:
Sundarnath Dham, also called Sundari Math, is a Shiva temple at Kursakanta in Araria district, Bihar, close to the India-Nepal border. Its worship centres on a Shivalinga that devotees believe to be self-manifested and which bears a swastika mark. The complex also has a Parvati shrine, a Ganesha image and a Nandi statue. Local tradition connects the site with the Mahabharata period and holds that the Pandavas worshipped here during their exile; this is folk belief and was not independently verified. According to a Nepali news report, King Kulanand Singh of Garhbanouli built a permanent temple in 1935, work on a larger one began in 2006 and resumed in 2012, and in 2016 a temple committee was registered with the Bihar State Religious Trust Board.
Wikipedia describes it as a major Shiva temple of the Mithila region, visited by Hindus from northern Bihar and southern Nepal, and classes its architecture as Nagara. Mahashivratri is the principal festival, with Shravan Mondays and Purnima also drawing worshippers; families in the border region also hold first-haircut ceremonies here.

description: Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, commonly called Patna Sahib, stands in Patna City, Bihar, and marks the birthplace of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, the tenth Sikh Guru, who was born there on 22 December 1666 and spent his early childhood in the city before moving to Anandpur. It is counted among the five Takhts, the Sikh seats of authority. Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji are also recorded as having visited Patna. According to the Sikh Encyclopedia, the inner sanctum is the room of the Guru's birth, and the earlier house on the site was rebuilt by Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1839. The 1934 Bihar earthquake badly damaged the building, and the present five-storeyed structure was completed in 1957. The shrine is administered by the Takhat Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib Prabandhak Committee; the Sikh Encyclopedia records that a committee took over from the earlier mahants in 1930 and a new constitution followed in 1956. Several smaller gurdwaras in the city are linked to the Guru's childhood, among them Bal Lila Maini Sangat and Gobind Bagh.

description: Vishnupad Temple stands on the bank of the Phalgu river in Gaya, Bihar, and is dedicated to Vishnu; the name means the temple of Vishnu's feet. Its sanctum holds a footprint of about 40 cm set in a basalt block and surrounded by a silver-plated basin. Tradition links the footprint to Vishnu's subduing of the demon Gayasura. The present structure is dated to 1787, when it was rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore. According to Wikipedia it is a shikhara-style building with an octagonal east-facing sanctum, a tower of roughly 30 metres, and walls of grey granite blocks joined by iron clamps, with eight rows of carved pillars supporting the pavilion. The temple is a centre for shraddha and pind daan rites, especially during Pitru Paksha, and an Akshayavat banyan tree within the complex is also associated with final rites. Gayawal Brahmins are its traditional priests.

description: Baidyanath Temple, also called Baba Baidyanath Dham, is a Shiva temple in Deoghar, in the Santhal Parganas region of Jharkhand. description: Shankaracharya Temple is a Shiva temple on a hill of the Zabarwan range overlooking Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, near Durganag and Dal Lake. The hill is also called Gopadri, and Takht-e-Sulaiman in some accounts. Kalhana's Rajatarangini credits King Gopaditya with building a temple there, according to Wikipedia, which also says the date is debated: Aurel Stein thought the superstructure recent but the base and stairs older. The shrine stands on an octagonal stone platform, and its dark circular sanctum holds a Shiva lingam. Kashmiri Hindu tradition holds that Adi Shankara visited the hill, which gave the temple its present name. Maharaja Gulab Singh is said to have built the stairs from the Durganag side. The Jammu and Kashmir Dharmarth Trust manages the temple, and Wikipedia reports that the site is also a centrally protected monument. Visitors climb a flight of several hundred steps or use a road up from Gagribal; security restrictions apply at the top.

description: Vaishno Devi is a cave shrine on Trikuta mountain near Katra in Reasi district, Jammu and Kashmir, at an altitude of about 5,200 feet. Pilgrims usually walk roughly 12 km from the base camp at Katra to reach it. Inside the cave there are no sculpted images; devotees have darshan of three natural rock formations called pindis, which Wikipedia describes as revered as the goddesses Mahakali, Mahalakshmi and Mahasaraswati. According to Wikipedia, the site was originally a place of worship for local communities who revered the three peaks, and the goddess later came to be identified as Vaishno Devi. Since August 1986 the shrine and the yatra have been administered by the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board, a statutory body constituted under the Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988. The Board reported about 9.5 million pilgrims in 2023, as cited by Wikipedia.

description: Bhoramdeo Temple stands near Chaura village, about 18 km from Kawardha town in Kabirdham district, Chhattisgarh, and is dedicated to Shiva. Scholars date the main stone temple to the 11th or 12th century on stylistic grounds; a pedestal inscription of 1098 CE and an inscription naming a king Gopaladev of a Naga dynasty are cited by Sahapedia as possible clues to its patron. The east-facing shrine has an entrance porch, a pillared hall and a sanctum, topped by an early shekhari-style tower. Its outer walls carry bands of lions and elephants and tiers of amorous couples, and Wikipedia notes that the complex is popularly called the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh. Niches inside hold Nataraja, Ganesha, Surya, Chamunda and Narasimha. According to Sahapedia, the present linga is not original, and the name Bhoramdeo is linked in some accounts to a Gond deity. Wikipedia notes the nearby Madwa Mahal, dated to 1349. Wikipedia's list of state-protected monuments includes the temple.

description: The Danteshwari Temple is in the town of Dantewada in southern Chhattisgarh, at the meeting of the Shankini and Dankini rivers, roughly 80 km from Jagdalpur. The town takes its name from the goddess Danteshwari, regarded as the presiding deity of the Bastar region. Tradition holds that the temple marks the place where a tooth of Sati fell, and it is listed among the 52 Shakti Peethas by Incredible India and Wikipedia, though the number of Shakti Peethas varies between traditions. Sources differ on its origin: one regional heritage page says the Chalukya rulers of Bastar brought the goddess from Warangal and built the temple in the 14th century, while another attributes it to the Kakatiya rulers. The sanctum is made up of a garbha griha and three mandapas, with a stone Garuda pillar opposite the entrance and a black stone image of the goddess inside. Bastar Dussehra, a long festival centred in Jagdalpur, is closely associated with her worship.

description: The Golden Pagoda, called Kongmu Kham in the Tai-Khamti language, is a Theravada Buddhist temple complex at Tengapani near Namsai in Arunachal Pradesh, on the banks of the Teang river. According to Wikipedia it is built in the Burmese style, was completed in 2010 and covers about 20 hectares; a 2019 report in NE Now says the project was initiated by Chowna Mein, then the state's deputy chief minister. Namsai's district website says a gilded Buddha statue modelled on the Kala Buddha of the Nalanda archive is enshrined inside, and that the grounds include a library, a monastery, a landscaped garden and a centre for cultural research on the Tai Khamti and Singpho communities. Kathina, the robe-offering ceremony, is the main festival, and Loi Krathong lamps are floated on a pond on its final day, according to Wikipedia. The same 2019 report cites over 100,000 visitors in a year, about 40 percent of them from abroad, mostly Thailand and Myanmar.

description: The Tripura Sundari Temple, locally called Matabari, stands on a small hilltop at Udaipur in Gomati district, Tripura, about 55 km from Agartala. Maharaja Dhanya Manikya is recorded as founding it around 1501, after a dream in which, according to local tradition, the goddess asked to be worshipped here. The hill's tortoise-like shape gives the site the name Kurma Pitha. The sanctum is a square Bengali-style structure under a conical dome, and the present building dates to the reign of Radhakishore Manikya, according to the state's temple trust page. The presiding goddess is worshipped as Tripura Sundari, also known as Shodashi, in a dark stone image, with a smaller image called Chhoto Maa beside her. The temple is counted among the 51 Shakti Peethas, where tradition holds that Sati's right foot fell. Kalyan Sagar lake lies beside the temple, and a large fair is held at Diwali. Since 2018 a state-constituted trust chaired by the Chief Minister oversees it.
